title: Clear and ambiguous
hookLine: some verses are clear, the foundation, others open to many meanings (3:7)
carry: some verses are for sitting with
last: NOT BEYOND WHAT I CAN BEAR.

cards: A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives the first two long surahs a shared nickname: the two bright ones. Al-Baqarah, just finished, and Al 'Imran, the Family of Imran, starting today.
Almost at once, before telling a single story, it stops to talk about reading itself. Not every verse in this book works the same way. Some are meant to be clear.
Some are meant to be lived with.

teach.b: Here's 3:7 in Pickthall's words. God has revealed the Scripture "wherein are clear revelations - they are the substance of the Book - and others (which are) allegorical."
The clear verses are muhkamat, from muhkam: made firm, tightly built. The root h-k-m also gives hikma, wisdom, and hakim, a judge.

The verse calls them umm al-kitab, literally the mother of the Book: the foundation everything else rests on. The others are mutashabihat, verses that resemble one another and can be read more than one way.
Then two kinds of readers. Those with a swerve in their hearts chase the ambiguous verses, looking for trouble and hunting a hidden meaning.
Those firmly rooted in knowledge say: we believe in it; all of it is from our Lord. The commentators have long discussed one detail.
The verse says no one knows its interpretation except God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge.
Where do you pause? Stop after God, and only God knows the meaning; the learned simply trust. Read straight on, and the learned know something of it too.

teach.h: ALL OF IT IS FROM OUR LORD.
teach.b: Respected scholars have held both, and both pauses are known in recitation.

Which verses count as ambiguous is discussed too: some name the letters that open certain surahs, some name verses about God's attributes, or the unseen. So the verse doesn't ask you to understand everything.
It gives you a floor to stand on, and permission to leave some verses open without forcing them.

how: Muslim scholars read the Qur'an's clear (muhkam) verses as its foundation and interpret the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses in their light; many ordinary believers simply affirm that all of it is from God and leave hard verses to further study.

o: a ruling handed down by a judge in court
made firm, clear, the solid ground of the Book
a verse that can be read more than one way

games.q: clear and ambiguous — tap the pairs.
p: verses open to more than one reading
the mother of the Book, its foundation

s: the Qur'an says every verse has one obvious meaning
3:7 itself says some verses are clear and others can be read more than one way.
muhkam shares a root with hikma, wisdom
scholars all pause in the same place in 3:7
some stop after God, some read on to those firmly rooted in knowledge; both are respected.

games.q: you reach a verse you can't make sense of. 3:7 describes two kinds of readers. which one does it praise?
o: the one who hunts for a hidden meaning to win an argument.
the one who says: we believe in it, all of it is from our Lord.
the one who skips it and never comes back.
games.why: those firmly rooted in knowledge say all of it is from our Lord. the verse warns about chasing ambiguous verses to stir up trouble.

practice: Bring to mind a line, from any book, that you don't understand or that troubles you a little, and hold it loosely, the way you'd hold something fragile that isn't yours, without arguing with it.
Then think of one line that's firm for you and let it be the ground you sit on: firm ground underneath, an open question in your hands.

wordCard.voice: Muhkam. Made firm, clear, tightly built. The muhkamat are the clear verses, the mother of the Book, from 3:7. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the firm, clear verses (3:7); singular muhkam, from the root h-k-m.

carryVoice: Your line: some verses are for sitting with. Not every question needs an answer today. Al 'Imran has begun.
